tagline: The fourth Gospel: the story of Jesus told as the eternal Word made flesh, written so that readers may believe and have life in his name.
overview:
John is the fourth of the four Gospels, the books that tell the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus. It covers the same ground as Matthew, Mark, and Luke, from John the Baptist to the empty tomb, but it tells the story from a different height. Before Jesus is born in Bethlehem or baptized in the Jordan, John takes the reader back to the beginning of everything and names Jesus as the Word who was with God and was God, through whom all things were made, who then became flesh and lived among us.

The first half of the book (chapters 1 to 12) is built around a series of signs, miracles that point beyond themselves to who Jesus is: water turned to wine, a boy healed at a distance, a man lame for thirty-eight years made to walk, five thousand fed, a man born blind given sight, and Lazarus raised from the dead. Around the signs come long conversations and arguments, with Nicodemus at night, a Samaritan woman at a well, and crowds and leaders at the Jerusalem feasts. The second half (chapters 13 to 21) slows almost to a stop. Five chapters are given to one evening, Jesus' last meal with his disciples, where he washes their feet, promises the Holy Spirit, and prays for them. Then come the arrest, the trial before Pilate, the crucifixion, the empty tomb, and the risen Jesus meeting Mary Magdalene, Thomas, and Peter.

It says most plainly what the other Gospels also claim: that in Jesus the God of Israel has come in person. It is also one of the simplest books in the New Testament to read and one of the deepest to study. Its vocabulary is small (light, life, truth, love, world, believe, abide, glory), and no one has reached the bottom of its thought. Many people have come to faith by reading it first, and it says openly that this is why it was written (20:31).
author:
The Gospel does not name its author. Its closing verses point to a figure it calls the disciple whom Jesus loved, who reclines beside Jesus at the Last Supper (13:23), stands at the cross (19:26), runs to the empty tomb (20:2-8), and is identified as the witness behind the book: “This is the disciple who testifies to these things and who has written them down. And we know that his testimony is true.” (21:24). The we in that verse suggests that others around the witness helped bring the book to its final form.

From the late second century the church identified this disciple as John the son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve and the brother of James. Irenaeus of Lyon, writing around AD 180, said that John the disciple of the Lord, who leaned on his breast, published the Gospel while living at Ephesus, and Irenaeus claimed a link to that generation through Polycarp of Smyrna. Many scholars still hold this view, pointing to the author's detailed knowledge of Jerusalem and Palestinian geography and to the curious fact that John son of Zebedee is never named in the Gospel.

Others think the beloved disciple was a follower of Jesus who was not one of the Twelve, perhaps a Jerusalem disciple, which would explain his access to the high priest's house (18:15-16). Papias, an early second-century bishop whose words survive through the historian Eusebius, mentions a John the Elder, and some (Richard Bauckham among them) identify the beloved disciple with this elder rather than with the son of Zebedee. A third approach, influential in the second half of the twentieth century and associated with Raymond Brown and J. Louis Martyn, reads the Gospel as the product of a Johannine community, a circle of churches shaped by the beloved disciple's testimony, whose own experience (including conflict with synagogue leaders) left its mark on the text as it was written and revised in stages. These views overlap more than they seem: nearly all agree that the book rests on the testimony of a remembered eyewitness and that it came to its final form among his followers.
date: Most scholars date the Gospel to the last decades of the first century, commonly the 90s, and many place it around AD 90 to 100. The reasons are the book's developed reflection on who Jesus is, its references to believers being put out of the synagogue (9:22, 12:42, 16:2), which many read as reflecting a time after the Jewish revolt and the fall of the temple in AD 70, and the early tradition that John wrote last of the four and lived into old age at Ephesus. The latest likely date is set by a small papyrus fragment of John 18, held in the John Rylands Library in Manchester and known as P52, which is usually dated to the first half of the second century, though the exact dating of such fragments is debated. A minority of scholars, including John A. T. Robinson, argued for a date before AD 70, noting that John 5:2 describes a pool in Jerusalem in the present tense and that the Gospel never mentions the temple's destruction.
setting:
The story is set in Judea, Samaria, and Galilee under Roman rule in the late 20s and early 30s AD. Herod the Great's temple, still being expanded, dominated Jerusalem. The high priests Annas and his son-in-law Caiaphas led the temple establishment, and Pontius Pilate governed Judea for Rome from AD 26 to 36. John is unusually attentive to the Jewish festivals: several Passovers (2:13, 6:4, 11:55), the Feast of Tabernacles (chapter 7), and the Feast of Dedication, now called Hanukkah (10:22). Much of the action takes place in Jerusalem, and the book knows its places well, from the pool of Bethesda to the Stone Pavement where Pilate sat in judgment.

The first readers lived a generation or more later, probably in and around Ephesus in the Roman province of Asia (western Turkey), if the early tradition is right. They were likely a mixed group of Jewish and Gentile believers. The Gospel explains Jewish customs and translates Aramaic words such as Rabbi and Messiah, which suggests that not every reader knew them. It also shows signs of a painful separation between the followers of Jesus and the synagogue. When the Gospel speaks of the Jews, it often means the religious authorities in Jerusalem who opposed Jesus, not the Jewish people as a whole: Jesus and all his first disciples were Jews, and Jesus himself says that salvation is from the Jews (4:22).
purpose: John states his purpose plainly near the end: “But these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name.” (20:31). The manuscripts differ slightly in the tense of the verb believe, and scholars debate whether the book was written mainly to bring outsiders to faith or to strengthen believers to keep believing. Both purposes fit the book, which has served as an evangelistic Gospel and as a book for the church's own deepening. It also answers the questions of a community under pressure: who Jesus really is, why his own people largely rejected him, what happens to his followers now that he has returned to the Father, and how they are to live in love for one another while the world hates them.
story: John opens with the first words of Genesis, “In the beginning”, and so places the story of Jesus at the start of everything, as the Word through whom the world was made. It then walks through the story of Israel in a new key: Jesus is the tabernacle where God's glory dwells (1:14), the new temple (2:21), the true bread from heaven given in the wilderness (chapter 6), the light and water of the Feast of Tabernacles (chapters 7 and 8), the good shepherd Ezekiel promised (chapter 10), and the Passover lamb (1:29, 19:36). The Gospel ends with the risen Jesus sending his disciples as the Father sent him and breathing the Spirit on them (20:21-22). The story continues in Acts, in the letters of John, and in Revelation, which the church has long associated with the same circle.
christ: Every Gospel is about Jesus, but John makes his identity the explicit subject of nearly every page. He is the Word who was God (1:1), the one and only Son who has made the Father known (1:18), the Lamb of God (1:29), and the Son of Man on whom heaven opens (1:51). Seven times he says I am with a picture attached: “I am the bread of life” (6:35), the light of the world (8:12), the gate for the sheep (10:7), the good shepherd (10:11), “I am the resurrection and the life” (11:25), “I am the way and the truth and the life” (14:6), and the true vine (15:1). Elsewhere he says I am with nothing after it, most strikingly “before Abraham was born, I am” (8:58), words his hearers take as a claim to the divine name, since they pick up stones. Yet John also shows the Son's full humanity more tenderly than any other Gospel: Jesus is tired at a well, weeps at a friend's tomb, and thirsts on the cross. The Word became flesh, and his glory is seen most fully when he is lifted up on the cross.
reading:
Read John slowly and listen for its double meanings. Words like born again or from above (3:3), living water (4:10), and lifted up (3:14, 12:32) carry two senses at once, and characters regularly hear the lower one while Jesus means the higher. Watch the misunderstandings, the signs, the feasts, and the hour that is not yet come and then arrives. Watch the characters too, who often stand for different responses to Jesus: Nicodemus, the Samaritan woman, the man born blind, Martha and Mary, Thomas, and Peter.

Two cautions help. First, John's language about the Jews has been misused to justify contempt for Jewish people, a grave misreading of a book written largely by and about Jews; the term usually names the Jerusalem authorities in their opposition. Second, the story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53-8:11) is not found in the earliest manuscripts and is printed in brackets in most modern Bibles, though many think it preserves a true memory of Jesus. Readers comparing John with the other Gospels will also notice differences in order and emphasis, such as the temple cleansing near the start rather than the end. Scholars debate whether John knew the other Gospels or wrote independently; either way, John writes with his own purpose and arranges his material to serve it.

structure.title: Prologue: the Word made flesh
structure.summary: A poem-like opening presents Jesus as the eternal Word, the agent of creation, the light rejected by his own and received by those who become children of God, and the one who has made the unseen Father known.

structure.title: The testimony of John and the first disciples
structure.summary: Opening with the marker “And this was John’s testimony” (1:19), a sequence of days shows the Baptist pointing to Jesus as the Lamb of God and the first disciples following him and naming him Messiah, Son of God, and King of Israel.

structure.title: From Cana to Cana
structure.summary: The Gospel numbers its first two signs, both done at Cana in Galilee (2:11, 4:54), and between them Jesus clears the temple, speaks with Nicodemus at night and a Samaritan woman at a well, and is received by Samaritans as Savior of the world.

structure.title: Signs and conflict at the feasts
structure.summary: The narrative is marked by Jewish festivals: an unnamed feast (5:1), Passover (6:4), Tabernacles (7:2), and Dedication (10:22). Jesus heals, feeds the crowds, and declares himself bread, light, and shepherd, and the section closes where the Gospel began, beyond the Jordan where John had first baptized (10:40-42).

structure.title: Lazarus raised and the hour arrives
structure.summary: The raising of Lazarus leads the council to plot Jesus' death. He is anointed at Bethany, enters Jerusalem, and announces that his hour has come (12:23). The public ministry closes with the narrator's verdict that despite so many signs many did not believe (12:37), and with Jesus' last public appeal.

structure.title: The farewell at the table
structure.summary: Marked by the words that Jesus knew his hour had come (13:1), this section gives one evening five chapters: the foot washing, the new command to love, the promise of the Holy Spirit, the vine and the branches, and Jesus' prayer for his followers.

structure.title: Arrest, cross, and resurrection
structure.summary: Jesus is arrested, tried before Annas and Pilate, crucified as King of the Jews, and buried. The risen Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene, to the disciples, and to Thomas, and the section closes with the Gospel's own statement of its purpose (20:30-31).

structure.title: Epilogue by the sea
structure.summary: After the purpose statement, a further chapter tells of a great catch of fish in Galilee, the restoration of Peter with a threefold question of love, and the beloved disciple, whose testimony stands behind the book (21:24). Many scholars regard it as an epilogue added in the final edition; it is found in every surviving manuscript.

themes.title: Believing and life
themes.body: The verb believe appears in John far more often than in any other Gospel, yet the noun faith never does. For John, believing is an act, a coming to Jesus, receiving him, and continuing in his word. Its result is life, eternal life, which John describes not only as endless existence after death but as a present sharing in the life of God that begins now and is completed in the resurrection.

themes.title: Signs and glory
themes.body: John calls Jesus' miracles signs because they point beyond themselves. Each reveals something of his glory, the visible weight and brightness of God's presence that Israel saw in the tabernacle and temple. The signs provoke both faith and opposition, and the Gospel suggests that faith resting only on miracles is fragile. The fullest display of glory comes, paradoxically, at the cross, when the Son is lifted up.

themes.title: Light and darkness, truth and the world
themes.body: John uses stark pairs: light and darkness, truth and falsehood, above and below, life and death. The world in John is God's creation, loved by him (3:16), but also humanity organized against him. These contrasts are not a dualism of two equal powers; the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it. They describe a crisis of decision that Jesus' coming brings.

themes.title: The Father, the Son, and the Spirit
themes.body: No Gospel says more about the relationship between the Father and the Son, who are one (10:30) and yet distinct, the Son sent by the Father and doing only what he sees the Father doing. In the farewell chapters Jesus promises another helper, the Holy Spirit, who will teach, remind, testify, and convict. The later church's doctrine of the Trinity drew heavily on this Gospel.

themes.title: Love and abiding
themes.body: The Father loves the Son, the Son loves his own to the end, and he commands his disciples to love one another as he has loved them. John's word for remaining or abiding describes a continuing, dependent union with Jesus, pictured as branches in a vine. Love for one another is the sign by which the world will know who his disciples are.

keyChapters.why: The prologue presents Jesus as the eternal Word made flesh, and the first witnesses name him Lamb of God, Messiah, and Son of God.
Jesus tells Nicodemus that one must be born from above, and the chapter contains the Bible's most quoted summary of the gospel, John 3:16.
After feeding five thousand, Jesus declares himself the bread of life, and many disciples turn away while Peter confesses that Jesus has the words of eternal life.
Jesus raises Lazarus after declaring himself the resurrection and the life, the sign that sets the plot to kill him in motion.
At his last meal Jesus washes his disciples' feet and gives the new command to love one another as he has loved them.
Jesus prays for himself, his disciples, and all who will believe through their word, that they may be one.
The empty tomb, the risen Jesus with Mary Magdalene and Thomas, and the Gospel's statement of its own purpose.

text:
John is one of the best attested books of the ancient world. The earliest surviving fragment of any New Testament book is usually thought to be P52, a scrap from a codex of John 18 in the John Rylands Library in Manchester, published by C. H. Roberts in 1935 and dated by most papyrologists to the second century, though Brent Nongbri (Harvard Theological Review, 2005) has shown how uncertain such dating is. Two papyrus codices from around AD 200 or somewhat later preserve much of the Gospel: P66 (Papyrus Bodmer II, in Geneva) and P75 (Papyrus Bodmer XIV-XV, which also contains Luke and has been in the Vatican Library since 2007). P75's text is strikingly close to that of Codex Vaticanus, copied about 150 years later, which shows how carefully one line of the text was transmitted. The great fourth-century codices Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, the fifth-century Alexandrinus and Bezae, and early translations into Latin, Syriac (including the Sinaitic palimpsest), and Coptic fill out the picture.

English Bibles differ at a handful of places. The King James Version was translated from the Textus Receptus, a printed Greek text descended from Erasmus's editions (from 1516) and based on late medieval manuscripts; modern versions follow critical editions built on the earliest witnesses. So the KJV includes the angel who stirred the water at the pool (5:3b-4), which is absent from P66, P75, Sinaiticus, and Vaticanus, and it reads ‘only begotten Son’ at 1:18 where the earliest manuscripts read ‘only begotten God’ or ‘one and only God’. The story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53-8:11) is absent from P66, P75, Sinaiticus, and Vaticanus, first appears in Codex Bezae, and in one family of later manuscripts (family 13) stands after Luke 21:38; modern Bibles print it in brackets with a note. At 1:34 some early witnesses read ‘the Chosen One of God’ for ‘the Son of God’, and at 20:31 the manuscripts divide between a present tense (that you may continue to believe) and an aorist (that you may come to believe). Chapter 21 is found in every manuscript, though many scholars think it was added in the final edition of the book.
reception:
John shaped Christian faith early and deeply. Its first known commentator was Heracleon, a Valentinian teacher around AD 170, and Gnostic teachers valued it, which may have made some church leaders wary of it for a time, though how much is debated; Epiphanius later reported a group he called the Alogi who rejected it. Irenaeus of Lyon (Against Heresies 3.1.1 and 3.11.8, around 180) defended the fourfold Gospel with John as a pillar, and Clement of Alexandria, as quoted by Eusebius (Ecclesiastical History 6.14.7), called it a spiritual Gospel written after the others had set down the outward facts. Origen's Commentary on John, Chrysostom's eighty-eight homilies, Augustine's 124 tractates, Cyril of Alexandria's commentary, and Theodore of Mopsuestia's commentary (preserved in Syriac) made it the Gospel of the great Trinitarian and Christological debates, from Nicaea (325) to Chalcedon (451). Augustine (Harmony of the Gospels 1.6) gave John the eagle as his emblem because he soars highest, and the eagle marks John in manuscripts such as the Book of Kells and the Lindisfarne Gospels and on countless lecterns.

Medieval readers treated John as the summit of Scripture: Thomas Aquinas lectured on it at Paris around 1270, and Meister Eckhart wrote a mystical commentary on it. Luther's 1522 Preface to the New Testament called John the chief Gospel, to be preferred to the others for its record of Christ's words, and Calvin's commentary (1553) called it the key that opens the others. In liturgy the prologue became the Gospel of Christmas Day in the West and of Easter in the East, and John's passion narrative is read on Good Friday in the Roman Rite. Johann Sebastian Bach set it in the St John Passion (first performed in Leipzig in 1724), and Arvo Pärt set it in his Passio (1982).

Modern criticism moved John from the center to the margin and partly back. Friedrich Schleiermacher preferred it as a source for Jesus, but David Friedrich Strauss (1835) treated it as largely mythical, and Ferdinand Christian Baur dated it to around 170. The publication of P52 in 1935 made so late a date impossible. Rudolf Bultmann's commentary (1941) read it through Gnostic myth; C. H. Dodd (1953 and 1963), Raymond Brown (1966-1970), and J. Louis Martyn (1968) turned attention to its Jewish setting and to the community behind it; and Richard Bauckham (Jesus and the Eyewitnesses, 2006) argued for its eyewitness basis. Jewish readers have pressed hard questions about the Gospel's language concerning the Jews, which was used for centuries to justify contempt and violence. The Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate (1965) rejected the charge that Jews then or now bear collective guilt for Christ's death, and Jewish scholars such as Adele Reinhartz have made John's portrayal of Jews a central question of modern study.

furtherReading.author: N. T. Wright
furtherReading.title: John for Everyone
furtherReading.note: Short passages with a fresh translation and warm, historically informed reflection, in two parts; the best place for a newcomer to begin.

furtherReading.author: Bruce Milne
furtherReading.title: The Message of John
furtherReading.note: A clear evangelical exposition by a pastor and theologian, written with preaching and personal study in mind.

furtherReading.author: Amy-Jill Levine and Marc Zvi Brettler, editors
furtherReading.title: The Jewish Annotated New Testament
furtherReading.note: Jewish scholars annotate the whole New Testament; Adele Reinhartz's notes on John explain its Jewish background and its language about the Jews (second edition 2017).

furtherReading.author: D. A. Carson
furtherReading.title: The Gospel according to John
furtherReading.note: A thorough evangelical commentary, strong on theology, the Greek text, and the case for the Gospel's historical reliability.

furtherReading.author: Marianne Meye Thompson
furtherReading.title: John: A Commentary
furtherReading.note: A balanced, readable mainline commentary with its own translation, especially good on John's picture of God.

furtherReading.author: Francis J. Moloney
furtherReading.title: The Gospel of John
furtherReading.note: A Roman Catholic commentary that follows the Gospel as a story, with close attention to its narrative design.

furtherReading.author: Joel C. Elowsky, editor
furtherReading.title: John 1-10
furtherReading.note: Selections from the church fathers, among them Origen, Chrysostom, Augustine, and Cyril, arranged verse by verse; a second volume covers chapters 11 to 21.

furtherReading.author: Thomas Aquinas
furtherReading.title: Commentary on the Gospel of John
furtherReading.note: Aquinas's thirteenth-century lectures on John in the translation by Fabian Larcher and James Weisheipl, reissued in three volumes by the Catholic University of America Press.

furtherReading.author: Raymond E. Brown
furtherReading.title: The Gospel according to John
furtherReading.note: A landmark two-volume commentary (1966 and 1970) by a Catholic scholar, rich in Jewish background and in the history of the text's composition.

furtherReading.author: Craig S. Keener
furtherReading.title: The Gospel of John: A Commentary
furtherReading.note: Two large volumes that gather the Jewish and Greco-Roman parallels to nearly every verse; the fullest guide to the Gospel's ancient setting.

furtherReading.author: C. H. Dodd
furtherReading.title: The Interpretation of the Fourth Gospel
furtherReading.note: A classic study of the Gospel's background in Judaism, Hellenistic thought, and early Christianity, followed by Historical Tradition in the Fourth Gospel (1963).

furtherReading.author: Rudolf Bultmann
furtherReading.title: The Gospel of John: A Commentary
furtherReading.note: The English translation of the most influential twentieth-century critical commentary (German original 1941), important for understanding the debates it provoked.

furtherReading.author: Richard Bauckham
furtherReading.title: Jesus and the Eyewitnesses
furtherReading.note: Argues that the Gospels rest on named eyewitness testimony and that John is the testimony of the beloved disciple, whom Bauckham identifies with John the Elder (second edition 2017).

furtherReading.author: Adele Reinhartz
furtherReading.title: Cast Out of the Covenant: Jews and Anti-Judaism in the Gospel of John
furtherReading.note: A Jewish New Testament scholar's sustained reading of how John presents Jews and Judaism, and a challenge to the expulsion theory of the Gospel's origin.

parts.body:
John is the fourth of the four Gospels, the books that tell the story of Jesus. It has 21 chapters. It covers the same ground as Matthew, Mark and Luke, from John the Baptist to the empty tomb. But it tells the story from a different height.

The other Gospels begin with a family tree, a birth, or a man preaching in the desert. John begins before the world was made: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (1:1). A few lines later comes the sentence the whole book hangs on: “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (1:14). The God who made everything has come to live as a man.

Then the story moves. Jesus turns water into wine at a wedding. He talks at night with a teacher named Nicodemus, and at noon with a Samaritan woman at a well. He heals, feeds a great crowd, gives sight to a man born blind, and calls his friend Lazarus out of a tomb. John calls these miracles ‘signs’, because each one points beyond itself to who Jesus is.

The second half slows almost to a stop. Five chapters (13 to 17) are given to one evening, Jesus' last meal with his friends. He washes their feet, tells them to love one another, promises the Holy Spirit, and prays for them. Then come the arrest, the cross, the empty tomb, and the risen Jesus with Mary Magdalene, Thomas and Peter.

John tells you plainly why he wrote: “so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name” (20:31). Its words are small and simple: light, life, love, truth, world, believe. Its thought is so deep that no reader has reached the bottom of it.

parts.h: Who wrote it, and how we know
parts.body:
The book does not give its writer's name. But it points to someone. Five times it speaks of ‘the disciple whom Jesus loved’. He leans against Jesus at the last supper (13:23). He stands at the cross beside Jesus' mother (19:26). He runs to the empty tomb (20:2). He is the first to know the risen Jesus by the lake (21:7), and Peter sees him following (21:20). At the very end the book says of him: “This is the disciple who testifies to these things and who has written them down. And we know that his testimony is true” (21:24).

Two things stand out in that verse. The book claims to rest on an eyewitness. And a group, ‘we’, speaks up for him. So many readers think others around this disciple helped bring the book into its final form.

Who was he? From the late second century the church gave a clear answer: John, the son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve and the brother of James. The strongest early witness is Irenaeus, a bishop in Lyon in Gaul (modern France), writing around AD 180. In his book Against Heresies (3.1.1) he says that John, the Lord's disciple who had leaned on his breast, gave out his Gospel while he was living at Ephesus in Asia, a great city on the west coast of modern Turkey. In another place (3.3.4) he says that John stayed at Ephesus until the time of the emperor Trajan. He also says that in his own youth he had seen Polycarp, a bishop whom apostles had appointed in Asia. So Irenaeus believed he stood only a short chain of memory away from the apostle.

There is a puzzle, though. Papias, a bishop in Asia early in the second century, wrote that he used to ask travellers what the Lord's disciples had said, and he names John among them. Then he names a second John, ‘the elder John’, beside a man called Aristion. His words survive only because the church historian Eusebius quoted them (Church History 3.39). Eusebius read Papias as speaking of two different men called John, and he noted a report of two tombs at Ephesus, both called John's. Irenaeus, earlier, seems to have read Papias as speaking of the apostle.

So there are several views today, and each has careful defenders. Many hold the old view: the beloved disciple is John son of Zebedee. They point to the writer's close knowledge of Jerusalem and the land, and to the odd fact that John son of Zebedee is never named in this Gospel, as if the writer kept his own name out. Others think the beloved disciple was a follower of Jesus from Jerusalem who was not one of the Twelve, perhaps John the elder. If he is the disciple ‘known to the high priest’ (18:15-16), that would fit. Others think the book grew in a circle of churches shaped by this disciple's witness, and was written and revised in stages.

What is tradition, and what is evidence? The evidence is the book's own claim (21:24) and its eye for places and times. The name John comes from tradition, early and strong, but not from the text itself. Nearly every view agrees on one thing: the book rests on the memory of someone who was there.

Most scholars date John to the last years of the first century, often the 90s. They give three reasons. The book shows long reflection on who Jesus is. It speaks three times of believers being put out of the synagogue (9:22, 12:42, 16:2), which many read as a sign of a later and painful split. And the early tradition says John wrote last of the four, when he was old.

A smaller group argues for a date before AD 70, the year the Romans destroyed the temple in Jerusalem. The best known is John A. T. Robinson, in Redating the New Testament (1976). He and others point out that John never mentions the temple's fall, and that one verse speaks in the present tense: “Now there is in Jerusalem near the Sheep Gate a pool” (5:2). Others answer that a storyteller can use the present tense, and that John had no need to mention the fall.

A small scrap of papyrus, the paper of the ancient world, sets a limit at the other end. It is called P52, and it is kept at the John Rylands Library in Manchester, England. It holds a few words from John 18:31-33 on one side and 18:37-38 on the other. It was bought in Egypt in 1920 by the scholar Bernard Grenfell and published by C. H. Roberts in 1935. Roberts dated its handwriting to the first half of the second century. That is why P52 is often called the oldest known piece of the New Testament.

Be careful with what P52 can show. Dating handwriting is not exact. Brent Nongbri (Harvard Theological Review, 2005) showed that hands like this one were used over a long period, so the scrap could be later than Roberts thought. P52 does show that John was being copied in Egypt, far from Ephesus, in the second century. It cannot tell us the year John was written.

Where was it written? The early tradition says Ephesus, and many scholars accept it, though the book itself does not say. For whom? The book explains Jewish customs and translates Aramaic words such as Rabbi and Messiah (1:38, 1:41), so not every first reader was a Jew from the land. It also seems to expect readers who already knew the story in outline, and believers under pressure. Its purpose in 20:31 fits both kinds of reader. The old copies differ slightly there, and the verb can mean ‘come to believe’ or ‘keep on believing’.

Read John straight after Mark, and you notice at once that it is different.

Much that the other Gospels tell is missing. John has no story of Jesus' birth. He does not tell the baptism as it happens; John the Baptist only describes it afterwards (1:32-34). There is no testing in the desert, no parable of the sower, no casting out of demons, no shining of Jesus on the mountain, and no bread and cup at the last supper. The phrase ‘the kingdom of God’, so common in the others, comes only twice (3:3, 3:5).

And much is found only in John: the wedding at Cana, Nicodemus, the Samaritan woman, the man ill for thirty-eight years at the pool, the man born blind, Lazarus raised, the foot washing, the long farewell of chapters 13 to 17, Thomas's cry, “My Lord and my God” (20:28), and the breakfast by the lake. Jesus speaks in long talks rather than short sayings, and the talks are often about himself.

Then there are three questions of timing.

First, the temple. Matthew, Mark and Luke put Jesus' clearing of the temple in his last week. John puts it near the start (2:13-22). Some think it happened twice: John has Jesus in Jerusalem at several feasts, and the words differ. Others think it happened once, and that John placed it early for reasons of his own, as a headline for the whole book. These notes do not settle it.

Second, the length of Jesus' work. Read on their own, the other three tell of one Passover, the one at which Jesus died. John names three (2:13, 6:4, 11:55). So John's story covers more than two years, and perhaps three if the unnamed feast of 5:1 was another. Many readers think the other three never set out to count years, and simply told the story as one road to Jerusalem.

Third, the day Jesus died. In Matthew, Mark and Luke the last supper is a Passover meal (Mark 14:12). In John, the morning after that supper the leaders will not enter the governor's palace, so that they can still ‘eat the Passover’ (18:28), and Jesus is condemned on ‘the day of Preparation for the Passover’ (19:14). So on John's telling Jesus dies on the day the Passover lambs were killed (Exodus 12:6). Some think John keeps the calendar and the others give the meal its Passover meaning. Some think John's phrases can be read to fit the others. Some think different groups kept the feast on different days. These notes do not choose; the notes on Mark 14 set out the views.

Did John know the other Gospels? Some scholars think he knew Mark, or Mark and Luke. Others think he wrote on his own, from a separate stream of memory. Either way, John is not a rival to the others. He tells of the same Jesus, with a different eye.

John is built with great care. Scholars usually see four parts.

The prologue (1:1-18) is the opening, like the overture before a play. It tells the reader in advance what the people in the story do not yet know: who Jesus is, and where he comes from.

The book of signs (1:19 to 12:50) tells of Jesus' work in public. It is built around seven signs: water turned into wine at Cana (2:1-11); a royal official's son healed from a distance (4:46-54); a man ill for thirty-eight years made to walk (5:1-9); five thousand fed (6:1-14); Jesus walking on the sea (6:16-21); a man born blind given sight (9:1-7); and Lazarus raised from the dead (11:1-44). Not everyone counts the same seven. Some fold the walk on the sea into the feeding, and some add the great catch of fish in chapter 21. John himself numbers only the first two (2:11, 4:54). Each sign leads to talk, and often to argument, about what it means. This half closes with a sad summary: “Although Jesus had performed so many signs in their presence, they still did not believe in Him” (12:37).

The book of glory (13:1 to 20:31) opens with the words ‘Jesus knew that His hour had come’ (13:1). It holds the last evening, the arrest, the trials, the cross and the resurrection, and it ends with the purpose of the whole book (20:30-31). The names ‘book of signs’ and ‘book of glory’ come from the scholar Raymond Brown, in his commentary of 1966 and 1970. C. H. Dodd called the second half ‘the book of the passion’.

The epilogue (chapter 21), a closing scene, comes after that ending. By the lake the risen Jesus gives the disciples a great catch of fish, cooks them breakfast, and three times asks Peter, “Simon son of John, do you love Me?” (21:16).

Running through the book are seven sayings in which Jesus says ‘I am’ and adds a picture: “I am the bread of life” (6:35); “I am the light of the world” (8:12); “I am the gate for the sheep” (10:7); “I am the good shepherd” (10:11); “I am the resurrection and the life” (11:25); “I am the way and the truth and the life” (14:6); and “I am the true vine” (15:1). Each picture takes something people cannot live without, bread, light, a way home, life itself, and says: this is what I am for you.

There are other ‘I am’ sayings with no picture added, and they may be the boldest of all: “before Abraham was born, I am” (8:58). The hard passages below come back to it.

The outline drawn at the top of this page breaks these four parts into eight smaller ones. Tap a part to see its chapters.

The Word made flesh. John's first claim is the biggest. The one who was with God in the beginning, through whom all things were made, became a human being (1:1-14). He was tired at a well (4:6). He wept at a friend's grave (11:35). On the cross he said, “I am thirsty” (19:28). John holds both together: truly God, and truly man.

Signs and belief. The verb ‘believe’ comes 98 times in John, nearly three times as often as in Matthew, Mark and Luke together. The noun ‘faith’ never comes at all. For John, believing is something you do: coming to Jesus, trusting him, staying with him. Signs can start it (2:11), but faith that only wants miracles is thin (2:23-25).

Life. ‘Eternal life’ in John is not only life after death. It is life with God that begins now: “Now this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent” (17:3).

Light and darkness. “The Light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it” (1:5). Nicodemus comes at night (3:2). When Judas leaves the supper, John says he “went out into the night” (13:30). John's pairs, light and darkness, truth and lies, above and below, are not two equal powers. They describe the choice that Jesus' coming sets before everyone.

The hour. At Cana Jesus says, “My hour has not yet come” (2:4). The phrase returns (7:30, 8:20) until, in Jerusalem, he says, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified” (12:23). The hour is his death, his rising, and his return to the Father.

Glory in the cross. Glory usually means honour and splendour. In John the glory of God is seen most clearly at the cross. Jesus speaks of being ‘lifted up’ (3:14, 12:32), and John explains that he said this to show the kind of death he would die (12:33). The cross is where he is lifted high.

The Spirit. Jesus promises ‘the Advocate’, the Holy Spirit, who will teach the disciples and remind them of everything he said (14:26). After rising, he breathes on them and says, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (20:22).

Abiding and love. ‘Abide’, or ‘remain’, is one of John's favourite words; it comes 40 times in the Greek of John. Jesus is the vine and his followers are the branches: “Remain in Me, and I will remain in you” (15:4). And the mark of his people is love: “As I have loved you, so you also must love one another” (13:34).

parts.h: The Old Testament and the feasts
parts.body:
John quotes the Old Testament less often than Matthew does, but it lies under every page. His first words, “In the beginning”, are the first words of Genesis. When he says the Word ‘made His dwelling among us’ (1:14), the Greek means ‘pitched his tent’. It recalls the tent in the wilderness, the tabernacle, which God's glory filled (Exodus 40:34). Jesus is the bread from heaven, like the manna (6:31-35). He will be lifted up like the bronze snake Moses set on a pole (3:14; Numbers 21:8-9). He is the good shepherd God promised in Ezekiel 34.

John also tells his story by Israel's calendar. The festivals are the book's clock.

Passover remembered how God brought Israel out of Egypt, and the lamb whose blood marked their doors (Exodus 12). John names three Passovers. John the Baptist calls Jesus ‘the Lamb of God’ (1:29). Near Passover Jesus feeds five thousand and speaks of himself as the bread from heaven (chapter 6). And he dies on the day of Preparation, with no bone broken, as was commanded for the lamb (19:36; Exodus 12:46).

Tabernacles, also called Booths, was the autumn harvest feast, when Israel lived in shelters to remember the years in the wilderness (Leviticus 23:42-43). The Mishnah, a book of Jewish teaching written down around AD 200, describes priests carrying water from the pool of Siloam to pour out at the altar during the feast, and great lamps lit in the temple's Court of the Women. How much of this was already done in Jesus' day is not certain. But on the last day of this feast Jesus cries out, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink” (7:37). Soon after he says, “I am the light of the world” (8:12).

Dedication, now called Hanukkah, remembered how the temple was cleansed and dedicated again in 164 BC, after a Greek king had defiled it (1 Maccabees 4:52-59). At that feast, in winter, Jesus walks in the temple and says, “I and the Father are one” (10:30). He calls himself the one ‘the Father sanctified and sent into the world’ (10:36). The word ‘sanctified’ means set apart for God, as the temple had been set apart again.

At each feast, Jesus stands where the feast was pointing. To picture the everyday Jewish world these feasts belonged to, the land, the temple, the Sabbath and the synagogue, see the guide to Jewish life in Jesus's day, listed under Go deeper at the end of this page.

John wrote in Greek, the common language of the eastern Roman world. His Greek is plain. His sentences are short and often joined by ‘and’. His words are everyday words, used again and again: world (78 times in the Greek of John), believe (98), life (36), love (44, as noun and verb), truth (25), light (23). But he loads these small words with great weight.

He likes words with two meanings, and he lets a listener pick the wrong one. Jesus tells Nicodemus that he must be born anōthen (3:3). The word can mean ‘again’ or ‘from above’. Nicodemus hears ‘again’, and asks how a grown man can enter his mother's womb a second time (3:4). Jesus means ‘from above’, from God, though that birth is also a second one. English Bibles divide: ‘born again’, as the Berean Standard Bible has it, or ‘born from above’.

Another is ‘lifted up’ (3:14, 8:28, 12:32). It can mean raised high in honour, or raised up on a cross. John says Jesus meant his death (12:33), and the reader is meant to hear both: the cross is where he is raised high.

There are more. ‘Living water’ (4:10) could mean fresh running water from a spring, or the life God gives; the Samaritan woman hears the first. ‘Spirit’ and ‘wind’ are the same Greek word, pneuma, and Jesus plays on it (3:8). And when the high priest Caiaphas says it is better for one man to die for the people (11:50), John notes that he was prophesying, saying more than he knew (11:51).

So read John slowly. When someone in the story misunderstands, stop and look again. John is about to say something deep.

In John the words ‘the Jews’ come about seventy times; the Greek word appears 71 times in the book. Often it names people who oppose Jesus. ‘The Jews’ question John the Baptist (1:19), argue with Jesus, pick up stones to stone him (10:31), and try to kill him (5:18). For centuries, many Christians read these verses as a verdict on the whole Jewish people, called Jews ‘Christ-killers’, and used John's words to justify contempt, expulsions and violence against Jews. This misuse is wrong, and the site rejects it plainly.

John does not support it. In his story the phrase means different people in different places. Often it means the Judean authorities in Jerusalem, the priests and leaders. It is ‘the Jews of Jerusalem’ who send priests and Levites to John (1:19). The parents of the man born blind are ‘afraid of the Jews’ (9:22), though they are Jews themselves. Sometimes it means a crowd, divided or curious: “there was division among the Jews” (10:19), and “many of the Jews who had come to Mary, and had seen what Jesus did, believed in Him” (11:45). Sometimes it simply means the people and their ways, with no hostility at all: ‘the Jewish Passover’ (2:13), ‘the Jewish rites of purification’ (2:6).

And nearly everyone in the story is Jewish. Jesus is a Jew; the Samaritan woman calls him one (4:9). His mother, his disciples, Nicodemus, Martha and Mary, and the writer himself are Jews. Jesus worships in the temple and keeps its feasts. And it is Jesus who says, “salvation is from the Jews” (4:22).

Why does John's language sound so sharp? Many scholars think the book was finished in a time of painful separation, when some Jews who believed in Jesus had been put out of their synagogues (9:22, 16:2). In 1968 J. Louis Martyn linked this to a synagogue prayer against heretics; many scholars now doubt that link. But most agree that this was first a quarrel inside one family. A family quarrel, written down, can sound harsh to people who were never in the family.

The Gospel's own teaching puts every reader inside the guilt. It was ‘the world’ that did not recognize him (1:10). The cross was carried out by Roman soldiers on a Roman governor's order. In Acts the first Christians pray that Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and the people of Israel all stood together against Jesus (Acts 4:27). In 1965 the Catholic Church's Second Vatican Council said that what happened in the passion ‘cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today’. Most churches teach the same.

Translators handle the phrase in different ways, and each has a reason. Some keep ‘the Jews’ everywhere, so that readers see what John wrote and learn to read it rightly. Some write ‘the Jewish leaders’ where the setting shows John means the authorities, so that no reader mistakes a few for a whole people. Some scholars argue for ‘the Judeans’, since the word first named the people of Judea; others answer that this cuts the link between the Jews of the Bible and Jewish people today. The Berean Standard Bible, quoted on this site, keeps ‘the Jews’. Whatever the wording, the meaning is the same: these are particular people in one story, not a people under a curse.

parts.h: Two passages, and what the old copies show
parts.body:
Two parts of John raise questions about how the book reached us. Neither changes any teaching of the Christian faith, and both are noted openly in modern Bibles.

The first is the woman caught in adultery (7:53 to 8:11). Teachers of the law bring a woman to Jesus and ask whether she should be stoned. He writes on the ground and says, “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her” (8:7). They leave one by one. Then he says to her, “Then neither do I condemn you,” and “Now go and sin no more” (8:11).

The oldest copies of John do not have this story. The early papyri P66 and P75, from around AD 200, and the great fourth-century books known as Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus go straight from 7:52 to 8:12. The first Greek copy known to include it is Codex Bezae, from the fifth century. Later copies place it in different spots: after John 7:36, at the very end of John, or after Luke 21:38. Jerome kept it in his Latin translation, and he said it was found in many Greek and Latin copies. So most scholars think it was not part of John at first. Many of them also think it is a true memory of Jesus, kept by the church and later written in here. That is why most Bibles keep it, in brackets or with a note. The Berean Standard Bible prints it.

The second is chapter 21. The book seems to end at 20:30-31, with its purpose. Then a new scene begins (21:1), and the book ends a second time (21:24-25), with a ‘we’ who vouch for the disciple. One verse corrects a rumour that this disciple would not die (21:23), which may mean he had died by the time it was written. Many scholars think chapter 21 was added in the book's final edition. But unlike the woman's story, chapter 21 is in every surviving copy of John that has the ending.

Neither question is a crisis. Both show that the church copied its Scriptures with care, and has always said openly where the copies differ.

parts.h: How the church has read John
parts.body:
Clement of Alexandria, a Christian teacher in Egypt in the late second century, passed on a tradition he had from the elders before him. The church historian Eusebius reports it (Church History 6.14.7). John wrote last of the four. He saw that the outward, bodily facts had been set out in the other Gospels. So, urged by his friends and moved by the Spirit, he wrote a ‘spiritual Gospel’. The phrase stuck. It does not mean that John cared less about what happened. It means he wrote to show what it meant.

The early church argued over who Jesus is with John in hand. At the Council of Nicaea (325) the church confessed that the Son is fully God, of one being with the Father. At the Council of Chalcedon (451) it confessed that he is one person, truly God and truly man. Both lean hard on John 1. Augustine preached 124 sermons on John, and gave John the eagle as his sign, because he soars highest. Thomas Aquinas lectured on it in Paris. Martin Luther called it the chief Gospel. John Calvin called it the key that opens the other three. Johann Sebastian Bach set its story of the passion to music, in the St John Passion, first performed in Leipzig in 1724.

Many people have come to faith by reading John before any other book of the Bible. That fits its own aim (20:31).

Modern scholars have argued over John more than over any other Gospel: whether it is history or reflection, early or late, the work of one eyewitness or of a circle of churches. Jewish scholars have pressed Christians to hear how John's words about ‘the Jews’ have sounded through the centuries. And careful readers, believing and not, keep returning to the book's own claim: that someone who was there saw, remembered, and wrote it down. “The one who saw it has testified to this, and his testimony is true” (19:35).

hard.line: ‘The Word was God’, or ‘a god’, as one translation has it? What the Greek says, explained in plain words.
Is Jesus rude to his mother when he calls her ‘Woman’? What the word meant then.
‘Born of water and the Spirit’: is the water baptism, natural birth, or the cleansing God promised in Ezekiel 36? Christians differ.
‘Eat the flesh and drink the blood’: is Jesus speaking of the Lord's Supper, of believing in him, or both? Churches read it differently.
The woman caught in adultery: is it part of John? What the old copies show, and why Bibles keep it.
‘You belong to your father, the devil’: hard words to particular opponents in a bitter argument. Never a word against the Jewish people.
‘Before Abraham was born, I am’: why his hearers picked up stones, and what ‘I am’ may echo.
‘I and the Father are one’: one in purpose, or one in being? How the church came to read it.
‘No one comes to the Father except through Me’: what it claims, and what Christians say about those who never heard.
‘The Father is greater than I’: does this make the Son less than God? How the creeds answer.
Forgiving sins and withholding forgiveness: what did Jesus give the disciples? Churches answer in different ways.
Thomas calls Jesus ‘my Lord and my God’, and Jesus accepts it. What a Jew meant by those words.
Who are the ‘we’ who vouch for the disciple's witness, and what does it say about who wrote the book?

words.line: Greek logos. God's speech, by which the world was made; in John, a name for the Son, who was with God and was God (1:1, 1:14).
John's word for Jesus' miracles: deeds that point beyond themselves to who he is. John records seven in his first half (2:11, 20:30).
To trust, to come to Jesus and stay with him. John uses the verb 98 times and the noun ‘faith’ not once (20:31).
Life with God that begins now and does not end: knowing the Father and the Son (3:16, 17:3).
God's truth and goodness shining into a dark world. Jesus calls himself the light of the world (1:5, 8:12).
The weight and brightness of God's presence. John sees it in Jesus, and most of all at the cross (1:14, 17:1).
The appointed time of Jesus' death, rising and return to the Father. ‘Not yet’ at first, then ‘it has come’ (2:4, 12:23).
Raised on a cross, and raised high in honour, both at once (3:14, 12:32-33).
Greek anōthen, which means both ‘again’ and ‘from above’: a new birth whose source is God (3:3, 3:7).
To remain, stay, live in. John's word for a lasting bond with Jesus, like a branch in a vine (15:4).
Often in John, people organized against God. Yet it is the world God loves (3:16, 15:18).
Greek paraklētos: one called alongside to help, plead for and comfort. John's name for the Holy Spirit (14:26).
In John often the Judean authorities in Jerusalem; sometimes the crowds, or simply the people. Never a verdict on a whole people (1:19, 4:22).

timeline.what: The temple is cleansed and dedicated again after a Greek king defiled it. Jews remember it at the Feast of Dedication, Hanukkah (10:22).
Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, rules Galilee and the land beyond the Jordan.
Antipas builds the city of Tiberias on the lake and names it for the emperor Tiberius. John calls the lake the Sea of Tiberias (6:1).
Pontius Pilate governs Judea for Rome. He tries Jesus (chapters 18 and 19).
John baptizes at Bethany beyond the Jordan and points to Jesus: ‘the Lamb of God’ (1:28-29).
Jesus clears the temple in Jerusalem and talks with Nicodemus at night (2:13 to 3:21).
At the pool of Bethesda, Jesus heals a man ill for thirty-eight years (5:1-9).
Near the lake, Jesus feeds five thousand and calls himself the bread of life (6:4, 6:35).
At the harvest feast Jesus offers living water and calls himself the light of the world (7:2, 7:37, 8:12).
In the temple Jesus says, ‘I and the Father are one’ (10:22-30).
Lazarus raised; the last supper; the cross on the day of Preparation; the empty tomb (11:55, 19:14, 20:1).
The two dates most often proposed for the crucifixion.
The risen Jesus meets his disciples by the Sea of Tiberias and restores Peter (21:1-19).
The Romans destroy Jerusalem and its temple.
The date most scholars give for the Gospel's final form. A smaller group argues for a date before 70.
Irenaeus writes that John gave out his Gospel while living at Ephesus.
The papyri P66 and P75 are copied; between them they hold most of John.
The scrap P52, with words from John 18, is bought in Egypt and then published by C. H. Roberts.

map.name: Capernaum
map.line: A fishing town on the lake. Jesus stays here with his family and disciples; a royal official's son lies sick here, and Jesus teaches in its synagogue (6:59).

map.name: Bethsaida
map.line: The home town of Philip, Andrew and Peter (1:44), near where the Jordan runs into the lake. Its exact site is disputed.

map.name: Tiberias
map.line: A new city built by Herod Antipas and named for the emperor. John calls the lake the Sea of Tiberias, where the risen Jesus meets his disciples (21:1).

map.name: Cana
map.line: Where water became wine, the first sign (2:1-11). Two sites claim it, Kafr Kanna and Khirbet Qana, a few miles apart; so it is placed roughly.

map.name: Sychar
map.line: A Samaritan town near Jacob's well, where Jesus talks with the woman at noon (4:5-42). Most place it at the village of Askar; some at old Shechem.

map.name: Bethany beyond the Jordan
map.line: Where John baptized (1:28). One site east of the river is marked as the place, but its identification is not certain, and other places have been proposed.

map.name: Jerusalem
map.line: The city of the temple and the feasts. Pools uncovered by archaeologists are widely taken to be Bethesda (5:2) and Siloam (9:7). Jesus dies outside its walls.

map.name: Bethany
map.line: The village of Martha, Mary and Lazarus, ‘a little less than two miles’ from Jerusalem (11:18). Here Lazarus is raised and Jesus anointed.
